In 1942, George Orwell penned a critique of T. S. Eliot’s Four Quartets.

It is remarkable, is it not, that a giant of 20th century literature was reviewing another? It makes me pine for that time.

The review is remarkable, too, for the insight it lends to the existential crisis of language. This is endemic to the broader malaise of modernity, a hollowing of the soul. As goes language, so goes humanity.

I am not talking about dialect; I am talking about the failure of our words, in all tongues, to communicate the essence of human existence.

Orwell lamented that there is “very little in Eliot’s later work that makes any deep impression on me”. Orwell wanted the Eliot of “The Waste Land”, “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” or “The Hollow Men”.

Orwell wanted the Eliot of passion, despair, desire. He wanted the Eliot who railed at the collapsing world of violence, war and totalitarianism.

Four Quartets, a compendium of four poems, was Eliot’s final work of poetry. It is the work of a man contemplating his mortality, pondering the meaning of time, the futility and fleeting beauty of life, the failure of poetry.

Eliot is not a man despondent; he is a man at peace, shading himself in the graveyard, what he called the life of significant soil. Personally, I consider Four Quartets Eliot’s crowning achievement. I think it is the greatest work of poetry of the 20th century. It is a profoundly spiritual work. Orwell hated it.

He accused Eliot of surrendering to the world. Orwell wrote, “there is faith, but not much hope, and certainly no enthusiasm”. Eliot’s later poems, Orwell said, “express a melancholy faith, and the earlier ones a glowing despair”.

Orwell believed we must rage. We must resent our mortality. Our resentment at death, he wrote, “is more likely to produce good literature than a religious faith which is not really felt at all”.

Eliot was writing to a higher God, however. He had gone beyond mere words.

Words strain,

Crack and sometimes break, under the burden…

Eliot now believed that words Decay with imprecision…

We were left with:

… the intolerable wrestle

With words and meanings. The poetry does not matter.

What mattered for Eliot was prayer.

And prayer is more

Than an order of words…

Orwell despaired at Eliot’s religious turn, saying: “The Church has not now any living imagery, any new vocabulary to offer.”

Orwell said Eliot’s poetry would have mattered more, had more to say, “if he could have found his way to some creed which did not start off by forcing one to believe the incredible”.

Orwell and Eliot have come to mind as I have contemplated Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence”.

Much has been written about the pope’s warnings of the perils of technology, but most have overlooked a crucial part of his message: our words are failing us.

His Holiness warned of the “Babel syndrome”. He defined this as “the idolatry of profit that sacrifices the weak, a uniformity that neutralizes differences, and the pretence that a single language – even a digital one – can translate everything, including the mystery of the person, into data and performance”.

Pope Leo called this a “dehumanization” that excludes God and turns us into machines. Technology, he says, “promises to free us from all weakness”, but leaves behind “entire populations”.

The modern world of tech imposes “a uniformity that eliminate[s] diversity” and values “homogenization over communion”. This modern Tower of Babel is a city built on pride and supposed self-sufficiency where “communication breaks down, languages are confused and people no longer understand each other. The result is not unity, but dispersion.”

This is the nihilism that German philosopher Martin Heidegger warned of when he wrote: “Beingness has dissolved into pure machination”.

Heidegger called this annihilation, a world of indifference. As he wrote: “A world that has become an unworld.”

To Heidegger, we are no longer people of language, we exist within language. Language defines our Being. Heidegger wrote: “[B]eing speaks everywhere and always, in every language.”

Through language we write a history that defines a people. The human being is never an individual but stands with a community.

Much has been written about the Pope’s warnings of the perils of technology, but most have overlooked a crucial part of his message: our words are failing us.

Now, Heidegger warned, we are subsumed within a language of technology. He blamed Ancient Greece, which, he argued, banished the mystery of the universe for a world of reason and mathematics.

This becomes the foundation of the modern West; a world, he said, grounded in a false truth.

Heidegger’s antipathy to what he saw as the delusions of modernity may go some way to explaining his attraction to the Nazis. Nothing could excuse his allegiance to Hitler. His writings reveal a vile anti-Semitism. Yet as a philosopher, he is unavoidable.

His writing on technology and language is prophetic. We have entered the world’s night, he said; God has fled, “divine radiance has become extinguished in the world’s history”.

The French philosopher Jean Vioulac calls Heidegger “the most radical thinker of our history”. Vioulac’s Apocalypse of Truth: Heideggerian Meditations is, to me, among the most profound books written on language, technology and the human spirit.

Vioulac believes the modern West is an apocalyptic project. It is built on absence: truth is not what is but what is not. Reason creates its own reality. It excludes the divine. We are mathematical, we are machinery.

“Our epoch,” he writes, “is the technological catastrophe, which is the threat of total annihilation as the consummation of the destiny of the West.”

Let me put it crudely: from the Greeks on, we have lived in a lie of truth. The world is what we can measure and make; it is not the world unseen. It is not a thing of the soul. There is another truth that is beyond reason, an untruth if you like, that is veiled by our rationality. Two-and-a-half thousand years after Plato, we need not fear the machines; we are the machines.

Vioulac is the link between Heidegger and Pope Leo. He writes about the Apostle Paul, who opposed the Greek wisdom of the world with “the wisdom of God”. As Paul says, “when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed” (2 Cor 3:16).

The New Testament, Vioulac says, “thematically develops the thought of an other truth”. It is a rival project to the mathematical machinery of the modern West. It is built, Vioulac writes, on the cornerstone of the “pathetic and singular flesh of the most humble”.

This is the truth Pope Leo speaks. It is a truth buried under the nihilism of modern rationality. It is a truth for which we find ourselves without language.

His Holiness says we must put aside the deceitful gods of technology. The common good, the pope says, “requires an evangelical language. We must avoid humiliating or antagonistic words, opting rather for a clarity that sheds light and a frankness that unlocks new possibilities.”

T. S. Eliot believed that prayer spoke more truthfully than poetry. The dead, he wrote, spoke a language unknown to the living. This was too much for George Orwell. He found it all too incredible.

Orwell left us a language of politics and a warning of dystopia. He would rail, no doubt, against the totalising of technology. We are living in his 1984. Yet Orwell gave us no words to save us.

Eliot, like Orwell, lived through the waste land. In Four Quartets, he told us:

We had the experience, but missed the meaning…

He left us a mystery, and a truth beyond time:

At the still point of the turning world … there the dance is…

Stan Grant is a theologian, writer and Charles Sturt University distinguished professor.
